title: Machine learning selects CSF and serum protein panels associated with early Alzheimer disease
summary: In a proteomic study, researchers measured paired CSF and serum samples in a discovery cohort and used random-forest machine learning to select a 19-protein CSF panel and an eight-protein serum panel to distinguish mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease from cognitively normal participants. Targeted proteomics verified candidate proteins in an independent multicenter cohort. In small held-out test groups, the CSF panel reached AUC 0.984 and the serum panel AUC 0.881; the CSF panel also distinguished Alzheimer-related MCI from frontotemporal dementia, ALS and Huntington disease in the reported analyses.
ai_technology: Random-forest machine-learning classifiers on CSF and serum proteomic profiles
organization: Capital Medical University; Westlake University, Zhejiang University and collaborating Chinese clinical institutions

evidence.tested: In a proteomic study, researchers measured paired CSF and serum samples in a discovery cohort and used random-forest machine learning to select a 19-protein CSF panel and an eight-protein serum panel to distinguish mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease from cognitively normal participants.
evidence.unknown: The AUC test sets were small (CSF: 9 Alzheimer-related MCI and 21 controls; serum: 8 and 21). The study used separate independent multicenter targeted-proteomics validation for candidate proteins; that does not make the small classifier test cohorts large or establish clinical utility. The serum panel was less effective at distinguishing Alzheimer-related MCI from other neurodegenerative diseases than the CSF panel. These are research panels, not routine tests.
evidence.ai_role: Random forests prioritized 19 CSF proteins and eight serum proteins to form disease-specific MCI classifiers after proteomic discovery and targeted validation; the selected panels were evaluated in held-out samples and against other neurodegenerative diseases.
